title: Financial Literacy and Investing
tagline: Budget, save, borrow wisely and start investing, with a working model for every idea
summary: Learn the money skills everyone needs: budgeting, saving and compounding, borrowing, inflation, the basics of investing and protecting what you have. Every module has a spreadsheet lab. Educational only: not personal financial advice.

modules.title: Money basics
modules.summary: Understand where money comes from and goes, and build a simple budget you can keep.
modules.outcome: You can list income and spending, separate needs from wants, build a monthly budget in a spreadsheet and explain how everyday banking tools work.
modules.intro: Financial skill starts with a simple habit: knowing where your money goes. This course is educational and general: it explains principles that apply anywhere, using rupee examples. It is not personal financial advice and cannot know your situation.

topics.title: Income, spending and the budget
topics.html:
Income is money you receive: pay, a stipend, pocket money, interest. Spending is money that leaves. The difference is what you can save: savings = income - spending.

Definition

Budget. A plan for how you will use your income over a period, usually a month, so spending serves your priorities instead of just happening.

A popular starting rule: 50/30/20
Share of incomeGoes toExamples
About 50%NeedsRent, food, transport, bills
About 30%WantsFun, eating out, subscriptions
About 20%Saving and debt repaymentEmergency fund, investing, loan payments
Watch out

50/30/20 is a rule of thumb, not a law. In a high-rent city needs may take more; adjust the shares but keep saving as a fixed line, not what is left over.

Check what you just learned

1. If income is 15,000 and spending is 12,400, savings are:
  • 12,400
  • 27,400
  • 2,600 (correct)
  • 0

Income minus spending.

2. In the 50/30/20 rule, 20% is for:
  • Wants
  • Tax
  • Rent
  • Saving and debt repayment (correct)

The 20% pays your future self.
keyPoints: Savings are income minus spending.
A budget is a plan; 50/30/20 is a starting guide, not a rule.

topics.title: Needs, wants and tracking
topics.html:
Sorting spending
GroupTestExamples
NeedsYou would struggle to live or work without itRent, basic food, transport to work, medicines
WantsYou would like it, but could do withoutTakeaway, new gadget, streaming
BothA need with a want attachedFood is a need; restaurant food is a want

Most overspending hides in small, repeated wants: a coffee, a delivery fee, a subscription you forgot. The cure is tracking: write down or log everything for one month. You do not have to judge; you only have to look.

A tracking habit

  1. Record every spend the same day, using an app or a notebook.
  2. Group spending into six to eight categories.
  3. At month end, total each category and compare it with your plan.
  4. Pick one category to reduce next month, not five.
Tip

Pay yourself first: move your saving into a separate account on payday, so the money is gone before you can spend it.

Check what you just learned

1. Which is mostly a want?
  • A monthly subscription to a game (correct)
  • Rent
  • Basic groceries
  • A bus pass for college

A subscription to entertainment is optional.

2. What does 'pay yourself first' mean?
  • Spend first
  • Set aside savings on payday before spending (correct)
  • Pay a friend
  • Skip saving

Saving happens before spending.
keyPoints: Needs are essential, wants are optional, and some items are both.
Tracking for a month shows where money really goes.

topics.title: Banking basics
topics.html:
Everyday money tools
ToolWhat it isKey point
Savings accountA bank account that pays small interestEasy access; low return
Debit card or UPISpends money you already haveCannot put you in debt
Credit cardBorrows from the bank to be repaid laterInterest is high if you do not repay in full
Net banking and appsManage accounts onlineGuard passwords and OTPs

A debit card takes money straight from your account. A credit card lends you money for up to about 50 days free of interest if you pay the whole bill by the due date; otherwise interest, often 30 to 40% a year, is charged.

Protect your money

  1. Never share your PIN, password or OTP, even with someone who says they are from the bank.
  2. Check your account statements monthly.
  3. Use apps from official sources and set a lock on your phone.
  4. Report a lost card or suspicious transaction at once.
Watch out

A bank will never ask you for your OTP or PIN. Anyone who does is a fraud.

Check what you just learned

1. Which carries a risk of expensive debt?
  • A debit card
  • A savings account
  • A credit card not paid in full (correct)
  • A UPI payment from your balance

Unpaid credit card balances attract high interest.

Key terms: flip and sort

Income
Money received
Budget
A plan for using income
Need
Spending that is essential
Want
Spending that is optional
Savings
Income minus spending
OTP
A one-time code; never share it
keyPoints: Debit spends your money; credit borrows the bank's.
Never share OTPs or PINs with anyone.

modules.title: Saving and compounding
modules.summary: Build an emergency fund and see why starting early beats saving more later.
modules.outcome: You can size an emergency fund, explain simple versus compound interest and use the rule of 72 to estimate doubling time.
modules.intro: Saving is not about giving things up; it is about giving your future self options. The other half is time: money left alone grows on its own growth. This module shows how.

topics.title: The emergency fund
topics.html:
Definition

Emergency fund. Money kept safe and easy to reach for surprises: a medical bill, a lost job, a broken phone. It is not for sales or holidays.

How big?
SituationTypical target
Student living with familyOne to three months of essential costs
Employed, single incomeThree to six months
Variable income or dependantsSix months or more
Worked example

A target in numbers

A family spends 24,000 a month and has 30,000 saved. The goal is six months.

  1. Target = 6 x 24,000 = 1,44,000.
  2. Months covered now = 30,000 / 24,000 = 1.25.
  3. Gap = 1,44,000 - 30,000 = 1,14,000.
  4. At 3,000 a month it takes 38 months.

Answer. A big goal is reached by a steady small habit; break it into milestones such as one month of costs, then three.

Tip

Keep the fund in a place where it is safe and available within a day, such as a savings account, not tied up in investments that can fall.

Check what you just learned

1. What is an emergency fund for?
  • Holidays
  • Investing in shares
  • Shopping sales
  • Unexpected essential costs (correct)

It covers surprises.
keyPoints: An emergency fund covers essential costs for three to six months.
Keep it safe and available, not invested for growth.

topics.title: Simple versus compound interest
topics.html:
Formula · Simple interest

balance after t years = P x (1 + r x t)

Interest is always on the original amount P.

Formula · Compound interest

balance after t years = P x (1 + r) to the power t

Each year's interest is added, so next year's interest is on the bigger amount.

10,000 at 8% a year
YearSimpleCompound
110,80010,800
211,60011,664
312,40012,597
413,20013,605
1018,00021,589

See compounding at work

Change the amount, the rate and the years. Compare simple and compound growth.

Adjust Amount invested (rupees), Yearly rate (%), Years and see Simple interest balance, Compound balance, Extra from compounding change.

The gap is small at first and then explodes. That is why time matters more than the rate: someone who starts early gets many more years of interest on interest.

Check what you just learned

1. Compound interest earns interest on:
  • The original amount plus past interest (correct)
  • Only the original amount
  • Nothing
  • The loan

Interest is added to the base.

2. Which matters more over decades?
  • A small rise in rate only
  • Time invested (correct)
  • The colour of the account
  • The bank's name

Time lets compounding work.
keyPoints: Simple interest uses the original amount; compound adds interest to the base.
The longer the time, the bigger the compounding effect.

topics.title: The rule of 72 and the cost of waiting
topics.html:
Formula · Rule of 72

years to double is about 72 / yearly rate in percent

A quick mental estimate: at 8% money doubles in about 9 years.

Doubling time
RateYears to double (approx.)
4%18
6%12
8%9
12%6
Worked example

Starting early versus late

Mia saves 2,000 a month from age 25 to 35 and then stops. Nitin saves 2,000 a month from 35 to 60. Both earn 8% a year.

  1. Mia puts in 2,40,000 over 10 years; the money then sits and keeps growing for 25 more years.
  2. Nitin puts in 6,00,000 over 25 years.
  3. At 60, Mia's money is typically about as large as, or larger than, Nitin's.

Answer. Starting ten years earlier can beat saving more for longer, because early money has more years to compound. (Illustrative: real returns vary and are not guaranteed.)

Watch out

The same rule works against you with debt. A balance at 36% interest doubles in about two years if you do not repay.

Check what you just learned

1. At 9% a year, money roughly doubles in about:
  • 4 years
  • 20 years
  • 8 years (correct)
  • 40 years

72 divided by 9 is 8.

Key terms: flip and sort

Emergency fund
Safe money for surprises
Simple interest
Interest on the original amount only
Compound interest
Interest on interest
Rule of 72
A quick doubling-time estimate
keyPoints: Years to double are about 72 divided by the rate.
Early saving needs less money than late saving.

modules.title: Borrowing and credit
modules.summary: Understand loans, EMIs and credit scores, and avoid the traps that make debt grow.
modules.outcome: You can calculate an EMI and the total cost of a loan, explain what a credit score is, and spot debt traps.
modules.intro: Borrowing is a tool: it lets you buy something now and pay for it over time. The price of that convenience is interest. Understanding exactly how much it costs is the difference between a useful loan and a trap.

topics.title: How a loan works
topics.html:
Definition

EMI. Equated Monthly Instalment: the fixed amount you pay each month, part of it interest and part repayment of the amount you borrowed (the principal).

Formula · EMI

EMI = P x r / (1 - (1 + r) to the power -n)

P is the loan, r the monthly rate (yearly rate / 12) and n the number of months. In a sheet: =PMT(rate/12, months, -loan).

Worked example

A 60,000 loan at 12% a year

Compare 12 and 24 months.

  1. 12 months: EMI is about 5,330, total repaid about 63,950, interest about 3,950.
  2. 24 months: EMI is about 2,825, total repaid about 67,800, interest about 7,800.
  3. The longer loan has a lower payment but costs almost double the interest.

Answer. A smaller monthly payment is not the same as a cheaper loan. Always look at the total cost.

Tip

Ask for three numbers before you sign: the interest rate, every fee, and the total you will repay.

Check what you just learned

1. A longer loan term usually means:
  • A lower rate
  • Higher payment, less interest
  • No interest
  • Lower payment, more total interest (correct)

Spreading the loan reduces each payment but adds interest.

2. Before borrowing, you should find out:
  • The rate, fees and total cost (correct)
  • Only the monthly payment
  • The bank colour
  • Nothing

The total cost shows the real price.
keyPoints: EMI = principal share plus interest share each month.
Longer loans have smaller payments but cost more interest.

topics.title: Credit scores and credit cards
topics.html:
A credit score is a number (in India often 300 to 900) that summarises how reliably you have repaid borrowed money. Lenders use it to decide whether to lend and at what rate.

What affects a score
FactorHelpsHurts
Payment historyPaying every bill on timeLate or missed payments
Credit useUsing a small part of your limitMaxing out cards
Length of historyOlder accounts kept in good orderMany new accounts at once
EnquiriesFew applicationsMany applications in a short time

Credit card habits

  1. Pay the full statement amount before the due date.
  2. Treat the card as a payment tool, not extra income.
  3. Keep use well below the limit.
  4. Set an automatic payment so you never pay late.
Watch out

Paying only the minimum keeps the account open but leaves the rest to attract interest, often 3% or more a month.

Check what you just learned

1. Which most improves a credit score?
  • Many new applications
  • Paying on time every month (correct)
  • Maxing out the card
  • Ignoring bills

Reliable repayment builds a record.
keyPoints: On-time payment is the biggest factor in a credit score.
Pay credit cards in full and use little of the limit.

topics.title: Debt traps
topics.html:
Common traps
TrapWhy it hurtsSafer move
Minimum payments onlyInterest piles up on the unpaid partPay in full, or as much as you can
Payday and app loans with huge feesEffective rates can be several hundred percent a yearAsk family or a bank; build an emergency fund
Borrowing to repay a loanDebt grows; you pay fees twiceTalk to the lender about a plan
Buy now, pay later without a planMany small instalments pile upAdd every instalment to your budget
Co-signing for a friendYou owe the debt if they stop payingOnly sign if you can afford the whole amount

Common mistakes

  • Looking only at the monthly payment.
  • Ignoring fees and penalty charges.
  • Taking a loan for something that loses value quickly, such as a night out.

If you are already in difficulty, speak to the lender early. Many have repayment plans. Free credit counselling services exist. Waiting almost always makes things worse.

Check what you just learned

1. What is the danger of paying only the minimum on a credit card?
  • No danger
  • The limit goes up
  • Interest builds on the rest (correct)
  • The score rises

The unpaid part keeps costing interest.

Key terms: flip and sort

Principal
The amount you borrowed
Interest
The price of borrowing
EMI
Fixed monthly payment
Credit score
A number summarising repayment reliability
Default
Failing to repay as agreed
keyPoints: Minimum payments and high-fee loans are the classic traps.
Talk to a lender early if repayments get hard.

modules.title: Inflation and real returns
modules.summary: See why prices rise, why 'safe' cash loses buying power and how to judge a return honestly.
modules.outcome: You can explain inflation, compute a real return and judge whether an investment beats rising prices.
modules.intro: 100 rupees today buys less than it did ten years ago. Inflation quietly shrinks the value of money, so a return only matters after you subtract it.

topics.title: What inflation is
topics.html:
Definition

Inflation. A general rise in prices over time, so each rupee buys less. It is measured as a percentage change a year.

What 100 rupees of groceries costs if prices rise 6% a year
AfterCost of the same basket
1 year106
5 years134
10 years179
20 years321

Inflation is not the same for everyone. If you spend mostly on food and fuel, your personal inflation may be higher than the headline figure. Education and medical costs often rise faster than average prices.

Tip

Think of inflation as a slow leak in a tyre: you notice it only when you check the pressure.

Check what you just learned

1. If inflation is 6% a year, a 100-rupee basket costs after one year:
  • 94
  • 100
  • 112
  • 106 (correct)

Prices rise by 6%.
keyPoints: Inflation reduces what each rupee buys.
Your personal inflation depends on what you spend on.

topics.title: Nominal and real returns
topics.html:
Formula · Real return

real = (1 + nominal) / (1 + inflation) - 1

A quick approximation: real is about nominal minus inflation.

A year at 6% inflation
Where the money sitsNominal returnReal returnBuying power
Cash at home0%-5.7%Falls
Savings account at 3%3%-2.8%Falls
Fixed deposit at 7%7%+0.9%Barely rises
Investment at 10%10%+3.8%Rises
Worked example

Is 5% good?

A deposit pays 5% when inflation is 7%.

  1. Real return = 1.05 / 1.07 - 1 = about -1.9%.
  2. After a year you have more rupees but can buy less.
  3. The deposit protects against losing the money, but not against losing value.

Answer. Always ask: after inflation, did my money grow?

Watch out

Taxes reduce returns too. A return that beats inflation before tax may not after tax. Check the rules that apply where you live.

Check what you just learned

1. A deposit pays 4% when inflation is 6%. Buying power:
  • Falls (correct)
  • Rises
  • Stays the same
  • Doubles

The real return is negative.
keyPoints: Real return is growth after inflation.
A return below inflation shrinks buying power even though the number rises.

topics.title: Cash, safety and growth
topics.html:
Cash is safe from market falls but is exposed to inflation. Investments can beat inflation but can fall in the short term. A sensible plan uses both, each for its own job.

Each money bucket has a job
BucketJobWhere it sits
Emergency fundBe there when neededSavings account
Short-term goals (under 3 years)Be there on a dateSavings account or fixed deposit
Long-term goals (10 years or more)Grow above inflationDiversified investments

A rule of thumb

  • Money you need within three years should not be exposed to big market swings.
  • Money you will not touch for ten years can accept ups and downs for higher expected growth.
  • Never invest your emergency fund.

Common mistakes

  • Keeping all long-term savings in cash for decades.
  • Putting money needed next year into a volatile investment.
  • Chasing last year's best performer.

Check what you just learned

1. Where does money needed in one year belong?
  • In a volatile investment
  • In a safe, accessible place (correct)
  • In a single company's shares
  • Nowhere

Short-term needs should avoid big swings.

Key terms: flip and sort

Inflation
A general rise in prices
Nominal return
Growth before inflation
Real return
Growth after inflation
Buying power
What a rupee can buy
keyPoints: Cash is safe from markets but not from inflation.
Match each pot of money to its time frame.

modules.title: Investing basics
modules.summary: Understand risk and return, the main asset types, diversification and regular investing.
modules.outcome: You can describe the main kinds of investment, explain the trade-off between risk and return and see how regular investing and diversification work.
modules.intro: Saving keeps your money; investing aims to grow it. Growth comes with risk: the chance that you get less than you hoped. This module explains the trade-off in plain terms. It does not recommend any product.

topics.title: Risk and return
topics.html:
Return is what you earn on an investment. Risk is the chance that the result differs from what you expected, especially the chance of loss. In general, higher expected returns come with higher risk. If someone offers high returns with no risk, it is a scam.

Risk, return and time
ChoiceRisk of lossTypical return pattern
Savings accountVery lowLow but steady
Fixed depositVery low (to the bank limit)Fixed, known
BondsLow to mediumRegular interest
Company sharesHigh in the short termHigher over long periods, with large swings
CryptocurrenciesVery highUnpredictable
Watch out

Past performance does not guarantee future results. A fund that did well last year may do badly next year.

Tip

Risk tolerance has two parts: how much you can afford to lose (your finances and time) and how much you can stand to lose without panic-selling.

Check what you just learned

1. A claim of high returns with no risk is:
  • Normal
  • Guaranteed
  • A scam warning sign (correct)
  • Legal advice

Genuine investments have risk.
keyPoints: Higher potential return means higher risk.
Risk includes how much you can afford and how you would react.

topics.title: The main kinds of investment
topics.html:
What each one is
TypeWhat you ownHow you may earn
Fixed depositA deposit with a bank for a termFixed interest
BondA loan to a government or companyRegular interest, then principal
Share (equity)A small part of a companyRising price and dividends
Mutual fund or ETFA basket of many investmentsDepends on what is in the basket
GoldA precious metalPrice changes over time
PropertyLand or buildingsRent and price changes

A mutual fund or an index fund pools money from many people and spreads it across many shares or bonds, so one failure does not sink you. Fees matter: a 1% yearly fee reduces returns noticeably over 30 years.

Common mistakes

  • Putting everything into one share or one trend.
  • Investing in something you do not understand.
  • Ignoring fees and charges.
Tip

Check that a seller or an advisor is registered with the official regulator in your country before giving any money.

Check what you just learned

1. A share represents:
  • A loan to a company
  • A tax
  • A deposit
  • Part ownership of a company (correct)

Shares are small parts of a business.

2. A mutual fund:
  • Pools money across many investments (correct)
  • Holds one company only
  • Is guaranteed
  • Pays no fees

It spreads risk across many holdings.
keyPoints: Deposits and bonds lend; shares own; funds pool many investments.
Fees and understanding matter.

topics.title: Diversification and regular investing
topics.html:
Definition

Diversification. Spreading money across many different investments so that a fall in one does not wreck the whole. 'Do not put all your eggs in one basket.'

Definition

SIP (regular investing). A systematic investment plan puts the same amount in at fixed intervals, such as every month, whatever the market is doing.

What regular investing can grow to (illustration)

Change the monthly amount, the assumed return and the years. The return is an assumption, not a promise.

Adjust Monthly amount (rupees), Assumed yearly return (%), Years and see Total you put in, Possible value (simple yearly approximation) change.

Why regular investing helps

  • It turns investing into a habit, not a decision to make each month.
  • You buy more units when prices are low and fewer when high (rupee-cost averaging).
  • It removes the temptation to time the market, which even experts fail at.
Watch out

Regular investing does not remove risk: values can still fall. It suits money you will not need for many years.

Check what you just learned

1. Diversification means:
  • Buying only one share
  • Spreading money across many investments (correct)
  • Selling everything
  • Borrowing

It reduces the damage from one failure.

Key terms: flip and sort

Risk
The chance of a result worse than expected
Return
What an investment earns
Diversification
Spreading across investments
SIP
Regular, fixed-amount investing
Index fund
A fund that copies a market index
keyPoints: Diversification spreads risk; regular investing builds a habit.
Illustrations assume returns that are not guaranteed.

modules.title: Protecting and planning
modules.summary: Insure against big risks, understand tax in general terms, spot scams and put it together in a plan.
modules.outcome: You can explain what insurance is for, recognise common scams, list your net worth and write a simple financial plan.
modules.intro: The last part of money skills is protection: not losing what you have built. It also pulls everything into a plan you can review each year.

topics.title: Insurance basics
topics.html:
Insurance transfers a risk you cannot afford to a company in return for a regular payment, the premium. You pay a small certain cost to avoid a large uncertain one.

Common kinds
InsuranceProtects against
HealthLarge medical bills
Term lifeLoss of income for dependants if you die
MotorDamage and third-party claims from a vehicle
Home or contentsFire, theft and similar loss

Buying sensibly

  1. Insure big risks you could not pay yourself, not small ones.
  2. Compare cover, exclusions and the claim process, not just the price.
  3. Pure protection (term insurance) is usually cheaper than products that mix insurance and investment.
  4. Read what is excluded before you sign.
Watch out

Never buy a policy because of pressure or a promise of guaranteed high returns. Check the exact benefits in writing.

Check what you just learned

1. What is a premium?
  • The payout
  • A tax
  • The regular payment for insurance (correct)
  • A bonus

It is the price of cover.
keyPoints: Insurance covers large risks you cannot afford yourself.
Compare cover and exclusions, not only price.

topics.title: Tax and scams
topics.html:
Tax rules differ by country and change often, so this lesson stays general. Income is usually taxed; some savings and investments receive special treatment; and some gains are taxed when you sell. Keep records and use the official government source or a qualified professional for the details that apply to you.

Habits that help with tax

  • Keep records of income, receipts and statements.
  • File your return on time every year.
  • Use official government websites, not links in messages.
  • Ask a qualified person when the rules are unclear.
Signs of a scam
SignExample
Guaranteed high returnsDouble your money in a month, no risk
Pressure to act nowOffer ends in 10 minutes
SecrecyDo not tell your family or bank
Request for OTP, PIN or remote accessI am from the bank, read me the code
Payment by unusual meansSend gift cards or crypto
Tip

If you feel rushed, stop. Call the real organisation using a number from its official website, not from the message.

Check what you just learned

1. Which is a scam sign?
  • A written fee schedule
  • A receipt
  • A registered company
  • Pressure to pay immediately (correct)

Urgency is a classic tactic.
keyPoints: Tax rules are local: use official sources.
Pressure, secrecy and guaranteed returns are scam signs.

topics.title: Net worth and your first plan
topics.html:
Formula · Net worth

net worth = assets - debts

Assets are what you own; debts are what you owe.

A plan has five lines
LineExample
GoalEmergency fund of 1,80,000 in 24 months
Monthly amount7,500 saved on payday
Where it sitsSavings account
Review dateEvery January
If life changesPause investing before pausing the emergency fund

Common mistakes

  • Having goals without amounts or dates.
  • Never reviewing the plan.
  • Investing before clearing very expensive debt.
Tip

Review once a year: update your net worth, check your savings rate and adjust the goals.

Check what you just learned

1. Net worth equals:
  • Assets minus debts (correct)
  • Income
  • Debts minus assets
  • Savings only

What you own less what you owe.

2. What should come before investing?
  • A holiday
  • An emergency fund and clearing very costly debt (correct)
  • Cryptocurrency
  • A new phone

Protect first, then grow.

Key terms: flip and sort

Insurance
Paying a premium to transfer a large risk
Premium
The regular price of insurance
Net worth
Assets minus debts
Scam
